utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-17/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The accused, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have appearances? The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Brenda Hollis with my colleagues Patricia Sellers and Michael Blaxill appear on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Luka Misetic and Sheldon Davidson on behalf of the Defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning the Court has just received filings from the Defence on notice pursuant to 94 bis (c) saying that they would like the expert witnesses in rebuttal to come and be cross-examined by the Prosecution. I don't know whether the Prosecution has received this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We just received it, Your Honour. However, we had anticipated doing direct exam of our experts, and they are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And also the second document is dealing with statements in rejoinder; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's not their witness in direct, it's their witness in rebuttal to our witness in direct, and ours is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- rejoinder. So we asked that we want to cross-examine their witnesses in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In rebuttal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have forgotten what the pending question was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear that because you have your responses to statements of Dr. Brown which are the rebuttal witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We wish to cross-examine both Dr. Brown and Dr. Rath, and then I believe the Court should have a notice that we wish to recall Dr. Morgan and Dr. Younggren in rejoinder following Dr. Rath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We have that. That's what we've just received as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Have the Prosecution received that, the rejoinder witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We just received that, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The proceedings this morning are for the reopening of the case pursuant to our decision of the 16th July, 1998. That is following disclosure of documents by the Prosecution after the proceedings were closed the last time in June. The order of proceedings the Trial Chamber feels will be as follows: There will be further cross-examination of those witnesses, Prosecution witnesses, recalled by the Defence, that is the first witness, Dr. Mujezinovic, and Witness A, and then they will be re-examined by the Prosecution; thereafter, the Defence will call their experts for examination-in-chief, then cross-examination by the Prosecution, re-examination; and thereafter the Prosecution will call their witnesses in rebuttal, the two experts, and re-examination in chief, then cross-examination and re-examination, if any, and rejoinder witnesses, if any, pursuant to the notice of the Defence. That is going to be the order of the proceedings. When it comes to times, we will adjust the afternoon sitting hours as we have started at 9.30 up to 12.30, and the afternoon we shall start at 14.30 to 17.30. There has been a change. We shall be sitting a half-hour later. And then we will have one break during the morning and one break during the afternoon. In the morning, it will be one break of 30 minutes at 11.00 hours and start at 11.30 up to 12.30. In the afternoon, I will be able to announce when we start at 14.30 to see how much time we need. We shall proceed accordingly. So I would ask the Defence which witness of the two they want to call first, to recall first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we intend to call Dr. Mujezinovic first, but we have some housekeeping matters to address before we get to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- some of which I believe will be uncontested, others which will likely be contested but we offer them right now. The first matter is that we wish to offer some of the statements that were produced to us into evidence; that is by consent of the Prosecution as well. I believe they are the statements of two doctors, who are unidentified in public so I won't use their names. These statements that were produced to us by Medica, the documents that were produced to us by Medica, we wish to offer those into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Those are the ones we dealt with in our decision, isn't it, where you asked for identities, the one the Prosecution said they didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, Your Honour, yes, we are going to offer those into evidence; I just haven't had the opportunity to make any copies, so I was going to offer them on a little later, but since the Prosecution and the Court already have copies, if you want to do that now, that's fine with me too, but it's the July -- the June disclosed documents, the two witness statements from the two doctors in Bosnia who briefly examined Witness A, the medical records that were produced to us pursuant to subpoena from Medica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we do that after the break when you're able to identify them clearly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then we can have the record clearly identifying the documents you wish submitted into evidence and then the Prosecution will also have time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- make sure that they are the ones they consented to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The other issue is that since we read the response or the statements of the Prosecution's expert witnesses, we realise that they are going to contend that we have no knowledge about treatment used at Medica with respect to how they proceed or anything about them. We searched our files, and we have two documents regarding Medica, the types of treatment it uses, its history, the amount of experience that the people at Medica had in treating patients generally of trauma and specifically with PTSD. That was a document that I downloaded off the internet and, as we sit here this morning, is no longer on the internet. The other document that we believe has evidentiary value and that our experts will comment on is the e-mail that was produced to the Court Thursday purported to be from Dr. Monika Hauser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Discussing what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is discussing the -- I don't know whether the Court has had an opportunity to see that or not, the e-mail that we faxed to the Court from Dr. Monika Hauser. It purports to be an e-mail from Dr. Monika Hauser. Our experts are going to comment specifically about the attitudes expressed in that e-mail and how those attitudes can affect a patient who is recovering from trauma. We wish to offer those into evidence. We rely on two grounds: First, the e-mail itself evidences the amount of cooperation that we could expect from Medica itself; second, the e-mail was only, according to its face, sent out on November 2nd, and therefore, it would be impossible to get someone to authenticate it; and third, there is precedent for this in the case of Prosecutor versus Blaskic, I believe the Prosecutor offered into evidence in July, it is my recollection, over 200 documents directly into evidence which Trial Chamber I admitted and notified the Defence in that case that they could review the documents if they wished to contest the authenticity of any of those documents, they could call witnesses to question the authenticity. Based on that precedent that is established in this Tribunal, we ask for the same -- it wouldn't be reciprocal, but the same consideration in this case. We believe it's directly relevant and, at the moment, is the only evidence of Medica, its history, et cetera, that is coming directly from Medica itself, in addition to the documents that were produced pursuant to subpoena. I have the documents here, Your Honours, if you wish to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we would like to see them so that we know exactly that we are dealing with the same documents. Have the Prosecution been given copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first document is entitled "BosNews Report - Medica Zenica - Women Therapy Centre"; the second document is entitled "Medica's Psycho Team - Finding Our Own Way"; and the third document is the e-mail purported to be from Dr. Monika Hauser who is the founder of Medica generally and specifically in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the Prosecutor -- they are just receiving the copies right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are just receiving them. We haven't seen these before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you need time to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there any one of them that had been produced, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, to give the Court its fullest information, we discovered these documents, one of which was stored away and we had no -- I had no knowledge of, or I had knowledge of but I had forgotten about. The other two -- and we discovered them Saturday night in preparing for the case, and so over the weekend, it would have been difficult to get the documents to the Prosecution. The other documents were put on the internet last week and were produced to the Court and I believe to counsel because they were filed by us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We were in contact with the Defence over the weekend, we gave them the phone number of Mr. Blaxill. We were here both Saturday and Sunday. To my knowledge, we didn't receive a phone call as to whether we were available to receive these. So our position is that we would have been available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it is clear then that the Prosecution would like some time to look at these before they can comment on whether or not they can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will deal with the matter later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In that case then, we will look at all the documents at a later stage. We can go ahead with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I wish to alert the Court that to the extent that we complete the examination of the witnesses before our morning break, those documents would be documents that I would want to use in the examination of our first expert, and therefore, I don't know how the Court would want to proceed with it, make a ruling while I'm proceeding or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me get you clear. You are saying some of the documents, you would like to refer them to your expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our experts have reviewed the documents and have comments about the documents, and the positions -- the techniques described in the documents as to the treatment of patients, there are certain admissions in the documents regarding experience or lack thereof in treating patients, so they would like to comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So all I want to know is: Are there any of these documents that you wish to refer to "A" or Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can proceed with those two at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can, Your Honour. Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which one would you like to have recalled first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Defence recalls Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Shall we go into closed session, depending on what examination you are going to proceed on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I leave that to the Court. It is the Defence's position that the testimony at least should be public, the issues are public. I think it would be to the benefit of not only my client specifically with respect to, quite frankly, the perception in the public about this case to date but, in addition, it would be beneficial to the public to hear what the testimony in the case is. That said, I leave it to you because I will announce to the Court today that almost all of the testimony with respect to Dr. Mujezinovic is going to be about Witness A. You know, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As long as no other names which were heard in closed session are going to be mentioned, then that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm completely aware of the requirements not to disclose names that are confidential, and I don't believe that Dr. Mujezinovic would have any reason to mention a name that is protected so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution requests that we do have this in closed session. When Dr. Mujezinovic testified as to issues that are relevant to why this case was re-opened during the initial phase of the proceedings, he testified in closed session. We believe that closed session is the only way to appropriately ensure that there are no statements that can be linked to Witness A if she is later identified, which we think is very possible. We are not aware of any perception of the fairness of this trial that would require otherwise appropriately closed session testimony to be given in open session. It would be our request that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond? First, I don't see how the Prosecution can say they don't see what the effect has been when Dr. Hauser posts on the internet that a war criminal is going on trial on Monday, so Mr. Furundzija has been convicted in the court of at least Medica's opinion. Second, the Prosecution had no objection to us talking about all of this in open session in final argument. These are all matters that are now in the public domain, and the only person it hurts, in terms of keeping these matters confidential, is my client. I would note the distinct disadvantage we're at because, much to my chagrin, someone from the Office of the Prosecutor made comments to the New York Times that the victim is being retraumatised by this Trial Chamber and by the Defence. We know for a fact that that is a request made by the Office of the Prosecutor in July to reopen the case and have Witness A come back. That is why our specific request is to at least have the testimony out in public so everyone can fairly comment upon this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But you do appreciate, Mr. Misetic, that part of the testimony of Dr. Mujezinovic during the trial proceedings was in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. It was at our request for a specific purpose, and that was so that Dr. Mujezinovic -- if I may backtrack? It wasn't because we were afraid that Dr. Mujezinovic would reveal something in terms of her psychiatric or psychological condition but that I was cross-examining him with respect to his knowledge about Witness A's spouse, and I didn't want her spouse's identity to become public. That was the motivation behind keeping it in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We feel compelled to request that, in closed session, the Defence tell us who it is he is asserting in the Office of the Prosecutor gave any information to any media. It is not the policy of the Office of the Prosecutor to provide any information to the media about ongoing cases, so we would request the specific name to whom the Defence is referring. We would ask for that in closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no need to go into closed session because there is no name. I suggest that the Office of the Prosecutor conduct an internal investigation because the person was specifically identified as an attorney who deals with sexual assault crimes at the Tribunal, and I assume that is not a Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you know very well that a media report without a name cannot be relied upon for your submission in court --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But I also understand the other side, which is it's very easy to keep yourself an unidentified source, make comments to the press, and then come into court and say you can't rely that the press actually used the correct statement. I have no problem with that, but this will then prevent the press from making false statements if the evidence is out in public, and that's the point of having a public trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The point, Mr. Misetic, here is that the Defence counsel cannot prove that it was somebody from the Prosecution's Office, (1), and you are relying on that to ask for open session. That is where the problem is, because you can't prove it. So the best thing for you is to withdraw that because you have agreed that there was no name so you don't actually know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I didn't give a name in the first place, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what if it was just a fabrication?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then we should call the New York Times reporter in and question her as to what her source is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is too far-fetched --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is not an important point, but it is -- it is what it is. I identified what her claim as to the source is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is not accepted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: After considering the issue whether or not Dr. Mujezinovic should be re-cross-examined in open or closed session, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the proceedings will go on in open session. So you may proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour? I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I forgot to raise an issue which may be of some importance and may be also something that the Prosecution wishes to consider. We would like to have our expert sit in to listen to the testimony of Dr. Mujezinovic and Witness A so that they can comment upon whatever evidence they hear directly in the courtroom. In addition, since neither Mr. Davidson nor I have any real expertise in the area of clinical and forensic psychology, to the extent that anything comes up for which we have not been prepared, they may be able to advise us as to a specific course of questioning which would be appropriate. We would have no objection if the Prosecution wish to have their experts also sit in so that they could comment upon the same testimony and rebut any testimony provided by our experts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We believe that it's not a matter of objection or no objection, it is a matter that is allowed by the Rules, and we would ask the same thing of our experts. We believe it can be of assistance to the counsel in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic, your experts can sit in. The same will be for the Prosecution witnesses in rebuttal; they can sit in from whatever stage so they can assist with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Our experts are in the Defence witness room. If the Court wishes to call them in, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we be assisted with that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe while we're waiting, the witness can make the solemn declaration due to the passage of time. So can the witness make a solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Court doesn't mind the experts being closer to the Defence counsel, right behind them. So that if there is need for consultation, it will be much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I believe it would be appropriate to indicate that on behalf of the defence are witnesses Dr. Jeffery Younggren and Dr. Charles A. Morgan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution can make its identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution expert witness present in court is Dr. Craig C. Rath, R-A-T-H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. If they both use English it's on channel 4. Yes, ready, you may proceed. Dr. Mujezinovic, you've been recalled for these proceedings, which are a reopening of these proceedings which were otherwise closed in June, for

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: whichever subject matter they will put to you. So you're here to answer the questions, and then after that the Prosecution will re-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Have you communicated with anyone about your testimony in this case since you've last testified in June of this year?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Have you communicated with Witness A since you last testified in this case in June of this year?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No. I haven't even seen Witness A.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Have you spoken with Dr. Kadrija Sabic about Witness A or this case since your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Do you know Mirha Pojskic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I know some Pojskics, but Mirhet or Mirheta I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I don't believe I said Mirheta, Doctor. I talking about the Mirha Pojskic, and perhaps this will refresh your recollection; Mirha Pojskic from Medica in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know her.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, wasn't it your testimony, in June, that you referred Witness A to Dr. Kadrija Racic-Sabic, and I'm citing page 208 of the transcript here: "Because she is specialised in these things, and I asked her to treat his wife. My lady colleague did this for a humanitarian organisation called Medica with a seat in Zenica. They had a team, and I cooperated with the team who helped those individuals who went through the post-war distress syndrome." Do you recall that testimony, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said last time that a person that the -- Person A came to my office. She spoke to me. I was unable to assist her, and I called up my colleague, whom I knew well, a neuropsychiatrist, Madam Kadrija Sabic-Haracic, who was at the same time an associate of Medica and who worked in the neuropsychiatric department in Zenica. I did cooperate with people from Medica, because after the end of hostilities with the Croats they would come to Stari Vitez. As Kadrija Sabic came with them I was introduced to her, but I didn't try to memorise her because there were several of them, you see. Kadrija Haracic was not the only one. It is possible that Mirha Pojskic was among them. I'm just saying there was a group of them, a team consisting of a sociologist, a gynaecologist, a psychiatrist, and I made it possible for them to have normal working conditions in Stari Vitez, and I did not interfere in their work. They had their own methods and programmes of work. I did not directly participate in their work with them. They would come in a van, and most of the examination were is done in the van itself or in my office -- or, rather, my surgery, because I would stop working when they came and pass over the office to them.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, you were the President of the War Presidency during 1993 and 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: And you were in Zenica after you were forced to leave the Vitez municipality in May of 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I was President of the War Presidency from the 2nd of February, 1993 until about November or December 1994. I was exchanged from Vitez on the 19th of May, 1993, and my family stayed behind in Vitez. They were exchanged on the 31st of May, and we lived with my sister in Zenica from the 31st of May for about six months, until I was given a house to live in by a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Is the answer to the question "Yes", Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I was President of the War Presidency of Vitez municipality, of the Bosniak, or as they say, the Muslim part of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: But from June 1, 1993 through December of 1994 you were in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: My family lived in Zenica. I spent a part of my time in Zenica, but most of my time in the villages of Poculica, Preocica, Vrhovine as a physician. I worked as a physician as well throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: As President of the War Presidency, did you become -- strike that. As President of the War Presidency did you ever meet Dr. Monika Hauser?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You never met Dr. Monika Hauser?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. I have heard of her. I know that she was in charge of Medica. And as far as I know, Medica, as an organisation, did a great deal in those parts helping the seriously traumatised people. I promised to the personnel that I would go and visit them, but I never did visit their premises. They told me where they were headquartered in Zenica, but I never went to those offices. But I do know that they did a great deal to help people, and that our official reports were highly laudatory of Medica. And privately, too, people had expressed their appreciation for what had been done by Medica in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Other than Witness A, did you ever refer a person or one of your patients to Medica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I advised -- I did advise other patients too, but Person A, in my view, was the most typical or, rather, a drastic case. I gave similar advice to others when they came to see me, that is, that they can seek assistance from them, because Dr. Kadrija Haracic was from Vitez, she was born in Vitez, and before the war and after the war we had collaborated when dealing with such and similar cases. Even today, as a physician, I often advise patients with this kind of disorder to address to Dr. Racic Sabic and her colleague, who is specialising on such problems, Emira.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You said you've worked with Dr. Racic Sabic prior to the war and after the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I said that we cooperated professionally, because the system of organisation of health care is such that I give specialist notice for a patient to go and see such and such a doctor, a specialist, "She will help you most."

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, but I'm asking you -- so then let's use your terminology. You cooperated with her during the war and after the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: So as the referring physician for Witness A, in these opportunities that you had to cooperate with Dr. Racic Sabic, did you ask -- let me finish the question. Did you ask for an update as to the condition of Witness A?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No. I had a lot of work to do. I didn't give such a note to Witness A. I said that she came to visit me in my office and not in my surgery, so I believed that the doctor would do everything she could to assist this person. And whoever I had sent there before the war, during the war and after the war never came back to me with any kind of complaint, or nobody ever told me that they were dissatisfied with the treatment they were given by this doctor. And since she took care of these people and monitored them for a longer period of time, mostly she would schedule check-ups on a regular basis, and she would follow their improvement. And as head of the Bosniak part of the municipality, Dr. Racic did once ask me to help with the transport of her patients to Zenica when she was unable to come to Vitez for these check-ups, and I did so whenever I could. I gave her -- would give her an ambulance or some other means of transport to Zenica where she worked.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, I think we may be having a translation problem. I'm not asking you formally, under your medical guidelines, whether you wrote a note to -- for Witness A to go visit Dr. Sabic, I'm asking you -- because you told Witness A to go see Dr. Sabic and you saw Dr. Sabic at various periods during the war and after the war, did you ever ask Dr. Sabic for an update of your relative, Witness A?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: As I said last time, Witness A, this woman, is a relative of mine. I asked about her when Dr. Sabic would come to Stari Vitez, because her parents lived there. And on one occasion she told me that it was a very serious case and that it would take a long period of psychiatric treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Did she tell you why she would need a long period of psychiatric treatment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: She told me that she was seriously psycho-traumatised person. We didn't go into the details because, as a doctor, as I'm a doctor of internal medicine, and Dr. Sabic's mother and father were my patients, and I had a lot of work, and people would come for examinations to see me very often. For a time I was alone in Vitez. The only doctor in the Bosniak part of Vitez for a time.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, did Dr. Sabic indicate to you that Witness A was suffering from depression?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that. She told me that she was a serious case of psychic trauma. No, we didn't go into any further details.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Did Dr. Sabic give you a prognosis for Witness A?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: That it would take long and that it would be very hard, the treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Did you ever see Witness A, personally, since May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That question has been put and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You asked the doctor whether he saw Witness A and he said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could the Court refresh my recollection as to what the answer was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It was, "No." You asked him, after he had testified here, after the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean to ask from May 1993 until the present, not from June 1998 till the present.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, let me repeat the question for you: Have you seen Witness A since -- strike that. You've already testified that you saw her in the fall of 1993 sometime when you referred her to Dr. Sabic. After the day that you referred her to Dr. Sabic. Did you ever have an opportunity to see her again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I saw her sons and husband, but I don't recall having seen Person A after that.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: How frequently would you see her sons and husband?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I said, the last time I testified, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, but one of our concerns that is arising is a variety of details appear to be coming out. Now, obviously we're in open session, and a number of family details relating to A Person are being related, and they might cause a problem in respect of the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection with respect to this limited portion of the testimony with respect to her husband and sons. If we go into closed session that's fine, all as long as we can go back into open session when I finish the questioning in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can go into closed session since you're continuing with the family details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can go into closed session. I understand the Registry says we can go into private session. So they shut off the sound without pulling down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we are in open session, so you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, in this mass of people, were a large portion of these people refugees from the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You answered one of my previous questions by saying that you were introduced to the staff of Medica and there was a mass of people, and I'm asking you, of that mass of people, was a large portion of those people refugees from the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: You mean I met the many people that worked at Medica?

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: That worked at Medica or that were patients at Medica.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how many patients there were in Medica from Vitez. I don't know that. I know that there were a number of patients, but I don't know their exact number. In Medica, as far as I know, they offered medical aid and assistance to all those asking for it, and as far as I know, they would go around the area; for example, they had a programme of work by which they would move from one locality to the next, they had a special vehicle, and they said beforehand they would give notice of when they would be arriving, and they would call their patients and then they would take in all the people who turned up in addition to the main office that was in Zenica; and how many patients they had from Vitez and how many refugees they had, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person named Marijana Senjak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Marijana Senjak. I know Krizan Senjak but not Marijana Senjak.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Do you know Nurka Babovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which individual you mean. Perhaps I do know the person, but I can't say. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Do you know who the Mujo Lama at Medica was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Do you know Sabiha Haskic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I know a lot of Haskics, but I don't know which Haskic you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Do you know a Haskic that worked at Medica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which individual with the surname Haskic works at Medica.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: How about an individual with the first name Sabiha at Medica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: The surname?

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Haskic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I know a lot of Haskics, but I don't know who Sabiha Haskic is. I never contacted Sabiha Haskic, had any contacts with a Sabiha Haskic when talking about Medica.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with the term "Post Traumatic Stress Disorder"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Post Traumatic Distress Syndrome, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Where did you learn about Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: While I studied medicine. I have read professional literature on the subject and that tests were made on the American soldiers in Vietnam, Post Traumatic Distress Syndrome and some other studies and reports which I received as professional literature.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You stated earlier that you were a specialist in industrial medicine when you testified in June. As part of that speciality, did you treat people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I graduated in 1984, internal medicine, and later on, I went on to specialise in industrial medicine and I worked with workers who were employed at special work posts and had jobs and specific conditions, workers working in the explosives factory or fuel departments for the production of various fuels.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Fine, Doctor. As I said, you indicated you worked in the field of industrial medicine, and I'm asking you, in that field, did you treat people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder or symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: You asked me that last time as well. We did not have, in our factory, people of that kind suffering from Post Traumatic Distress Syndrome. There was an explosion in 1985, but we did not have any cases of PTSD. Because there were systematic regular check-ups for all the employees, this was compulsory by law, and for each individual worker, in addition to the examination I would conduct for these particular jobs, they would undergo an examination by a neuropsychiatrist and an eye doctor and, if necessary, other specialists as well, and we would draw up reports every year on the results of these periodical regular check-ups for all the employees working in the Vitez factories, and you can receive copies of these reports, if you wish, with my signature on them.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm interested in how you determined that you didn't have any of these cases. What methodology did you use to evaluate a person to determine whether or not they had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, all these doubtful cases were examined by a neuropsychiatrist and his opinion was final. All the cases where there was any doubt, all the cases that we thought might be suffering from psychiatric disorders, we would send these individuals to consultations with psychiatrists and psychologists; and if we receive a positive answer when they did the psycho tests and if the psychiatrist ascertained that these individuals suffered from psychological disorders or were traumatised psychologically in any way, then all these workers would be sent to have their labour capabilities assessed. They wouldn't carry on with their jobs until they had undergone these examinations to see whether they were capable or not, and this was normal standard procedure according to the rules and the law.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Okay. But, Doctor, you did the initial intake to determine whether or not these were doubtful cases for you to refer on to the neuropsychiatrist, and what I'm asking you is: In that initial intake procedure, what factors did you look at -- what was your methodology in determining whether or not this person had the symptoms of PTSD which would necessitate a referral to a neuropsychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I said that we did not have in our reports cases of this kind, but wherever there was any doubt that -- because at these jobs, you had to have completely healthy individuals working there, and we would hold consultations and this was normal, standard medical procedure, that a psychological test must be carried out, we consulted psychologists to see what type of disorder we were dealing with and whether that particular individual could carry on with his particular job.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I understand that, Doctor, and that's my point. Are you saying that you would only look at the person and, based on your intuition or gut feeling, you would refer them or not refer them, or are you saying there were specific criteria that you were given to make an evaluation and then make a referral?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, let me explain one thing to you. I examined each individual from head to toe. That is a basic examination. And it is basics in medicine that you take the general clinical picture of each individual to see whether he suffers from insomnia, whether he has nightmares, whether he has bouts of perspiration. So all these are standard symptoms that we look at. And if any of these symptoms deviated from the norm, then we would, by law, consult a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to get at, Doctor. So could you tell us what specifically were the symptoms -- what were the symptoms themselves? I understand you did your job and you did it the best you could, but I'm asking you to list what the symptoms were that you would evaluate, and based on your evaluation of those symptoms, you would make a referral on to the neuropsychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: We would send them to specialists -- for example, if we thought somebody had become a chronic alcoholic, if he failed to turn up regularly at work, we would look into these reasons to see what was amiss; and on the basis of their case histories, if they had any fears, anxieties, difficulty in sleeping, if the individual heard noises, if they suffered from hallucinations of any kind, and if they did, we would send these individuals for a psycho test and for psychiatric treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. With respect to those symptoms, were those symptoms official symptoms that were published in Yugoslavia or some place else by a medical association in terms of that this was the clinical evaluation or these were the symptoms of PTSD, or were you just generally looking at people's psychological and psychiatric health and then making referrals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I examined the individuals. I would take the particulars and their case history. We had a team of people in the factory that dealt with preventive medicine. I was the president of the team. There was the social worker, there was a sociologist, and there was a psychologist on the team. For each individual person, for each individual case, my colleague and myself, and she was a specialist in industrial medicine, I was president of the group, and we would see what should be done, what preventive measures should be taken to stop any further deterioration in the health of the employees.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, in Yugoslavia, were there professional associations or state institutions that established standards of care for physicians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Please, sir. We would get certificates guaranteeing that we could perform our work. If I graduated from the school of medicine, I would get a diploma. If I graduated from the specialist training course, I would again receive a diploma allowing me to perform my work.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I think we're having a problem understanding each other. I'm not referring to your qualifications, I'm saying, in the field of medicine, with respect to illnesses, diseases, any other problems that a person would have, were there professional associations or state institutions that would evaluate illnesses, diseases, et cetera, and establish criteria for physicians to look at and to be able to make an official diagnosis that was approved by the physicians or the professional association or the state institution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: (No interpretation)

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're familiar with organisations like the American Medical Association or British Society of Psychologists, I believe it's called, these medical associations that meet to establish guidelines for particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon my interruption, Your Honours, but there appears to be no interpretation to the previous answer, according to my machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript does show "No interpretation." I wonder why. Maybe Mr. Misetic can repeat the question because you seem to have a problem with the witness identifying what it is that you're trying to ask him about, so if you can just repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The problem is going to be, Your Honour, that his answer didn't match my question to begin with, so I don't know whether it's going to help. I'm doing a follow-up question anyway, if counsel doesn't mind, I'm still on the same topic, trying to explain it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You are familiar with organisations like the American Medical Association and the British Society of Psychologists? Were there similar organisations or state institutions in Yugoslavia that established criteria for physicians to use in treating patients; in other words, for example, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, the Yugoslavia Society of Physicians has established that these are the six or seven or eight or ten criteria that a physician should evaluate, and if ten are present, the person has Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, we had, at a local level, an association of physicians, and then we had an Association of Physicians of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they did not have the function of the type of association in America and Switzerland. We had special teams, and when we would examine individuals, as -- my particular speciality was prevention. If I doubted, if I had any doubts, then this would be verified by a psychiatrist or psychiatric hospital. After that, they would -- the team to assess the working capability of these individuals would come to a conclusion; and our criteria, for the most part, we used Western literature. We based our criteria on the criteria found in Western literature. Now, you asked me about the criteria. Well, we, of course, read various medical journals and received information, but it was my job to have doubts. It was never official that that was so. This had to be ascertained either by sending the individual to hospital, usually the patient was hospitalised, and that is what we do today as well. So these people are sent to a psychiatric hospital and their state is followed up for a certain period of time, at least 15 days. And so a team of physicians working in the hospital, officially they would examine the individual, come to a -- arrive at a diagnosis, and this is the diagnosis that a patient would receive when being discharged from the hospital. That's the system.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I think we're getting a little off track. With respect to the local unions of physicians and the union of physicians at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did either of those institutions actually establish guidelines for you and other physicians in the practice of medicine?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: The Association of Physicians of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or our municipality of Travnik, this is what we did -- an individual physician, for example, I listened to a lecture by Mrs. Racic Sabic about Post Traumatic Distress Syndrome, she held a lecture for the physicians of Travnik municipality, and I attended that lecture which was held at the Kruscica Motel. So she would hold a set of lectures for the physicians of the Travnik region and she would discuss the criteria and the treatment for the disease. She was invited. She was a physician working in Zenica. She is a member of the Association of the Physicians of Zenica, and she was invited by our region to hold a lecture of this kind because that is her speciality. You can ask her for a copy of her lecture. I attended the lecture, and she presented this specialist lecture for physicians. She told us her visions of Post Traumatic Stress Syndromes, how to look at the disease, how to treat it, and that is how the Association of Physicians still function in Bosnia-Herzegovina today.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Let's talk about this lecture on Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we've reached the time when we should have our break this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. It's an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you still need more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You still have more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're going into a new field, and this is an appropriate time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber shall break for 30 minutes. We shall resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic. You indicated that you still have a lot of questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But I'm afraid that we're going into general issues instead of evidence regarding the treatment received by Witness A, because this doctor didn't deal with Witness A. So what other areas are you intending to cover?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are foundational areas for both Witness A and for the other experts in the case. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please keep to the limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I intend to keep to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, also for the record, this is dealing specifically with lectures of what appears to be the treating physician on the topic in issue, and since we don't have the treating physician here this is the next best thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Dr. Mujenznovic, you indicated that you attended lectures given by Dr. Kadrija Sabic about Post Traumatic Stress Disorder in the city of Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not. I said that Dr. Kadrija Sabic-Haracic, at the invitation of the doctors' section of Travnik, did deliver a lecture, in the Kruscica Motel in Vitez, for all physicians. The topic of the lecture being Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: And you said you attended that lecture?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I attended, and I was one of the organisers -- or, rather, sponsors of that gathering among the lecturers, because Dr. Haracic-Sabic was not the only lecturer. There were others on other topical issues in medicine.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, I want to clarify the record here.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. With respect to this topic --

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, I need to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: -- experience were is also presented --

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You were referring to the doctor as Dr. Kadrija Sabic-Haracic, do you mean Dr. Kadrija Racic Sabic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the same topic, a lecture was delivered in Kruscica, in this motel in Vitez by Dr. Dzenana Cvjetic, a neuropsychiatrist from Travnik. Her lecture was devoted to the same topic, and on the same day, for all physicians, be they general practitioners or specialists in various fields.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: And when was this lecture given?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you the exact date, but it was in 1995. But it was held and this can be easily verified.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You say 1995. First, did Dr. Sabic indicate why this was an important topic and when, if you can, so I don't have to ask you too many questions, when she started doing work in this area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You're familiar with what the contents of her lecture are; are you not? What the contents were, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No. I listened, as did the other doctors present, to the lectures of these two doctors on this subject.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You listened because you wanted to increase your own knowledge in the profession; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: It is customary for the physicians' association to invite certain doctors, certain specialists to discuss the most topical issues in medicine, so that experiences, observations, personal experiences, the experiences in which that particular doctor is employed may be presented. These meetings were customary among doctors of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then they would go from one town to another. Every month such lectures would be organised in another town to discuss the latest issues in various areas of medicine.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: And Post Traumatic Stress Disorder was topical, I presume, because of the war and the effects it was having on the citizens and residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: At the time it was a topical issue, because the doctors came across difficulties of this kind among their patients, and they wanted to hear from somebody who was most competent in that field and who could present views as to the way in which those patients should be treated, tell us how they treated them and what the results were, how successful that treatment was. The substance of the lecture was that; that is, to familiarise all the doctors present with these things and to advise doctors, who were not so familiar with these matters, to refer to these two doctors. One was in Travnik and the other in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You said that they were talking about how these people should be treated. What did they say about how these people should be treated? Specifically, what did Dr. Sabic say about how these people should be treated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: You see, I can tell you in broad lines that the treatment is protracted and difficult, that psychotherapy is required, together with medication. That would be a global answer. As for the details, I wouldn't go into them, because I don't think I'm competent enough to talk about these things. The main aim was to draw our attention that there was, in Travnik, Dr. Dzenana Cvjetic; and in Zenica, Dr. Sabic-Haracic, who said that she has been working on these problems for some time now in the Medica humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, doctor, I'm asking you to be an expert in the area, I'm asking you to recall the contents of that lecture, on that particular date when you attended, with respect to what Dr. Sabic had to say.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I think I told you the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: That's correct. With respect to that lecture, did Dr. Sabic indicate what proportion of the population suffers or was suffering from PTSD, from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you exactly, but they did say that she was very busy, that she had a lot of work, that the treatment, in some cases, was more difficult than in others, that there were differences regarding the consequences. I don't remember the percentage that she cited. I don't think she did mention any names. She didn't mention any specific name in her lecture.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: What did Dr. Sabic tell you to look for? What symptoms in a patient that could indicate Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that question? Because it's as if I was asking -- answering questions in school.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I'll ask the questions, you answer the questions, and if there's an objection --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: It's as if you were testing me in my knowledge of medicine.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Let's be perfectly clear. I don't want to offend you. I'm not asking you about your knowledge of an area, I understand you're not a specialist in the area. I'm asking you because you're a witness, not in your capacity as a doctor, what you recall about Dr. Sabic's words. There's a difference in what I'm asking you, and I'm asking you these questions not to ask about your knowledge, but to ask about Dr. Sabic's knowledge. So could you please tell us what Dr. Sabic told you what to look for in trying to evaluate whether a person has Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Dr. Sabic delivered an extensive lecture about her experiences, and she said that individuals had come to see her, as well as -- see her personally, as well as through the Medica humanitarian organisation. Among the symptoms she mentioned were fear, nightmares, insecurity, feelings of there being no aim in life, that people had disturbed personalities, that they find it very difficult to adjust to normal life, that they felt a certain shame, that they were ashamed of their very selves as we like to say, that they feel when they meet someone, that people were only thing about what they felt rather than any other characteristic that they had as individuals. So those were the symptoms that she mentioned in most part. That people just couldn't fit in. They couldn't resume a normal life, that they felt everything was a heavy burden. And as in Bosnia, most people, regardless of ethnicity, have been brought up in a patriarchal spirit. People are very closely linked to their families. As for soldiers, she would say that some of them would commit suicide, just like that, without any immediate cause. They would simply withdraw, stop communicating with their surroundings and they would suddenly commit suicide. And the environment in which those people lived, knew them as exemplary citizens, and they just couldn't understand what was happening, because such tendencies were not widespread in Bosnia before. A normal person who had a job, his family, that simply everything was breaking up, and this was an added difficulty to the already difficult situation for that particular individual. The doctor said that the treatment was difficult, that rehabilitation needed to be -- needed a great deal of time, that they needed encouragement, that they needed to be told that they were not alone in this situation, that they needed to be told that other people too had gone through similar difficulties, that one had to continue to live to try and restore their stability, their families, the normal course of life for the benefit of themselves and their families. This is a very rough rendering of what she said. I can assure you that the doctor's presentation was far better, more precise, with greater detail, that that is not my particular field of interest. For me, this was sufficient to be able to refer people to the right place as soon as I noticed that they needed treatment of this kind.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, just to know, I appreciate your effort in recalling your memory, and that's all we're trying to establish here. With respect to the treatment that you talked about, what specific types of treatments did she note could be used with patients of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that the most important part of the treatment is psychotherapy, combined with certain medicines, pharmaceuticals, which would repress fear, which would provide relaxation. But the main treatment was psychotherapy.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Did she talk about what they did in psychotherapy? What types of treatment within psychotherapy did they use?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot reproduce what she said.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I would suggest there's no problem in you obtaining a copy of that lecture. The doctor would be glad to give you a copy, I'm sure, if you ask for it.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: On the odd chance that we don't get a copy of that document, can you just tell us what your recollection is about what types of treatment within psychotherapy she said were employed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. I have already indicated, in broad lines, to encourage people, to talk to them at length, to approach them very gradually in the psychotherapeutic sense, not to go to the event immediately, but to start in a roundabout way, in very broad lines, and only gradually to focus in on the problem itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We've heard that before. We're going into too many --

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier that you examined -- I should say you met with Witness A sometime, you believe, in the fall of 1993, perhaps the winter of 1994, at which time you referred her to Dr. Sabic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I said that Person A came, accompanied by someone, I can't remember who it was, to see me. That is what I said. I was not in my surgery in which I used to work, but I was in an office -- in my office. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: But my point is that you did meet with her and refer her to Dr. Sabic? I'm just trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we're wasting a lot of time in repetitions. It was there before, it's been there this morning. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just wrap up then.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: Doctor, you testified that at that referral meeting that she was incoherent, that she cried, that she couldn't put together coherent sentences. Is there anything else you recall about that meeting in terms of the symptoms that she had, especially now looking back, in terms of what you know about the symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I can tell you now, and I think that is also what I said in my previous testimony, that I was, after all, surprised by the woman's appearance. She had completely changed. She had become deformed. She was a very good looking woman, a very attractive woman, a beautiful woman, in her middle age, a middle-aged woman, who had worked in Vitez as a salesperson. She dressed very elegantly, and who was always very neat. So it was a shock when I saw her, for me. I asked Person A, "What on earth happened to you?" As I was treating her parents and her family, I told you that we were related, she tried to tell me that some terrible things had happened to her. I went on to say that she started telling me what had happened to her, but after a sentence or two she started weeping, and I may have spent about half an hour with her. I told her that there was a doctor, Kadrija Haracic, and that I would personally call her up by phone and ask her to receive her. I also had the telephone number in the neuropsychiatric department and her home number, and I called the doctor and asked her to see her immediately, because I said that this was an urgent psychiatric case. After that I did not see Person A.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: You said urgent psychiatric case and I understand the events of what happened, but I'm asking you now to talk specifically about symptoms, especially since you have an understanding of what the symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder are. Can you recall if any of those symptoms were present at the time you referred her? If you want, I can give you some examples and you can giver me a "yes" or "no" answer, if that will make it easier.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Mrs. A, as I already said, shocked me by her appearance. She appeared frightened, exhausted. Mrs. A, as I said, when she started telling me what it was, she would say, "Doctor, you don't know what I've been through. You don't know what happened to me. I don't know what to do. I want to kill myself. I'm ashamed. I can't sleep, I have nightmares. I can't calm down. I cannot -- I cannot talk to people. Everything irritates me." I told you that she thought everyone was staring at her, and that everybody was accusing her of something, that her sons are already big, grown up,

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon the interruption, but once again we're having concerns here regarding the protective measures situation. We're in open session again. This is delving back into sufficient family relationship that I think could lead to unfortunate, if inadvertent, identification of the person concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then I just ask the witness not to speak --

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE REGARDING
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about symptoms, Doctor, so please don't any comments about the husband or the sons. Do you recall any other symptoms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Look, if as a doctor with some 20 years of experience behind me, in any profession, including my own, there are many things that one knows from experience and that I could see. If I called up the doctor to ask her to receive her immediately, that the woman wanted to commit suicide, then I think I've told you enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I have just a second, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to consult. Your Honour, we've completed our cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I do have a few the matters, Your Honours. They will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Firstly, I would just like to confirm the time period when this encounter with the person concerned took place. You stated in your testimony, I believe in June and again this morning, that that was late 1993 or early 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the second half of 1993, that period, the latter half of '93. The autumn of '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In point of fact, the specialist lecture you attended in relation to Post Traumatic Stress Disorder itself took place later in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, two physician specialists. I mentioned Dr. Kadrija Sabic Haracic and Dr. Dzenana Cvjetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At the end of 1993, did you, when you referred the person to your psychiatry colleague, did you offer any kind of formal diagnosis or assessment of that person when you referred her?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I promised Person A that I would personally contact the doctor. I was not in my surgery, I was in an official room, and at the time, I was President of the Wartime Presidency, and I said that I would do everything to try and locate her and to have her receive Person A for treatment, but I did not give any official referral note for a hospital because I did not have the papers for that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you offer any diagnosis yourself or a medical opinion on the condition of Person A to the doctor to whom you referred her?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I have already stated, and I conveyed this to the doctor, that the person in question was in a very difficult psychological state, distressed, and that she had tendencies towards suicide and that she should be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, sir, after that date, have any part in her treatment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I did not, and I don't consider myself to be competent for treating individuals of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, a few moments ago, you made reference to the person to whom you referred and you used the words "Kadrija Haracic." Can you perhaps confirm again the name of the psychiatrist to whom you referred or clarify if there's any confusion over the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I've already clarified that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I asked: You were using this name. Do you mean Kadrija Racic Sabic? And he answered "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: The person is a woman, I think she was born in 1952. She is a woman, she's not a man. She is Haracic Sabic. Her maiden name is Haracic and her surname, her husband's surname, is Sabic. I think that that is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: She has three daughters. What more can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have amply answered that question. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I was going to say -- may I just say that that concludes my re-examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we need clarification because he made that mistake before, and I asked him whether that is Kadrija Racic Sabic and he indicated "Yes," and I would just like to know whether that is still the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: With regard to which one? The last name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just want to avoid a situation where the Prosecution comes in at the end and says now we're talking about another person, not Kadrija Racic Sabic but Kadrija Haracic Sabic and that that might be somebody else, and I would just like to make sure that we're clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, on two occasions now you've used the name Kadrija Racic Sabic. You used that name when you testified in June of this year --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I never said Racic, I said Haracic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you like to see a copy of your transcript, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There could have been a spelling mistake.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: Please. I have always referred to the person as Haracic, Haracic, and not Racic, but Haracic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can I pull up the transcript here in this case where I asked him not 45 minutes ago -- okay. Just as long as, for the Court, it doesn't matter. That's fine with me. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know what you have in your transcript, but I kept saying Sabic Haracic and I said that her maiden name was Haracic, and she is married and her married surname is Sabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. Any reasons why the witness should not be released? Anything from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think certainly based on the -- what we are aware of the Defence case at this point in time, our comment would be "No." We would see no objection. Of course, things could change.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. You are released. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
