utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we can continue before the lunch break. We have some twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are going into closed session. Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we are going into closed session with all the blinds down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We're going to open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do that, we believe that part of our argument concerning the e-mail from Dr. Hauser would go into matters that are confidential matters as to our argument, so we would ask if that issue is going to be dealt with now, that we remain in closed session. That is to say, Your Honour, that part of our argument is going to go into the subpoena and compliance with the subpoena. Those were confidential filings, and that's the reason I raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that we'll begin with those matters that will be discussed in opened session, and later on we'll move to closed session, such as the documents you are discussing right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In that regard, Your Honour, concerning the testimony of the witnesses that are about to testify, because of what we consider very serious concerns about identifying data that will disclose them in open session today, the Prosecution would again request that portions of testimony that these witnesses would give about Witness A would be in closed session. Again, whether it's inadvertence or whether it's by plan, if identifying data comes out in closed session, it really does detract from the protective measures in place. We believe there will be general data, but regarding Witness A, again we would ask that that be in closed session. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the best way to deal with that, as the evidence is narrated and after counsel leading the witness, whether that be examination-in-chief or cross-examination, to indicate the matters to be discussed will require closed session, then we'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate we'll be talking about these documents, so out of formality I tender the documents to the clerk so that they can be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just clearly, so for the record, identify them one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first document being tendered is titled "Medica's Psycho-team, Finding Our Own Way." The second is titled, "Put Pressure On The Hague Trial Against War Criminal Because of Sexualised Violence Threatens To Overturn." And the third is by stipulation, the parties have agreed to admit the documents produced to the Court pursuant to subpoena by Medica, and it is titled -- the text -- well, my first page has as the first line, "The text of the report typed for the sake of legibility," and beneath that, "24, December, 1993." It should be marked as confidential, because the -- Witness A's name is disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document will be marked D22, the second D23 and the third D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that was taken off the Internet, the first document described by the Defence, which I believe is D23 -- D23?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: D32 we have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: D22, the document taken off the Internet, we have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The second document, which is the e-mail from Dr. Hauser that was previously submitted to the Trial Chamber in a pleading from the Defence dated 5 November, 1998, we object to that document. The third document, the text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What are your reasons for objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's what I mentioned would involve talking about a confidential matter. Basically I will tell you, Your Honour, that the basis would be relevance and confusion of issues. The argument relates to a confidential matter. The third document, the text, we have no objection to. We do note that earlier the Defence had spoken of an Internet document that we were given a copy of. That has not been mentioned. So we would ask clarification if that that is a document that will not be offered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think so far the Defence is only asking that these three -- Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify. Learned counsel is correct, and I do have those stacks, and I would like to move this document into evidence as well. There are matters within that document that discuss mission statements. I believe that's been tendered to the Court, if I'm not mistaken, this morning. Mr. Bos may -- no? Well, I tender it to the Court, and I ask it be marked as Exhibit D25, and note that the Prosecution has indicated that they have received a copy. Your Honour, for the record may I indicate that the D25 is be titled, "Bos News Report Medica Zenica Women Therapy Centre."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May I ask, is he getting a photocopy?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to D25.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic, D23 was objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'd move it into evidence, Your Honour, and because counsel has indicated they wanted to argue this in closed session, I leave it to the Court, first, to indicate whether -- to make a ruling on that and then I'll proceed to make my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will now go into closed session to discuss the objection by the Prosecution of document D23. Yes. We don't need to turn down the blinds. So just wait until we are informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Doctor, will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Jeffrey Nels Younggren, Y-O-U-N-G-G-R-E-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your residence?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I live in Rancho Palos Verdes, California, in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I am a clinical and forensic psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where did you receive your education?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I received my education at the University of Arizona, Tucson, Arizona, in the United States, my master's degree in psychology there and my Ph.D. in clinical psychology there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever served in any military?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which military did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I served 29 years as a commissioned officer in the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever received a medal while you served in the United States Army?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I most recently received my second Meritorious Service Medal for contributions to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your current role with the United States military?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I serve as United States Army Reserve clinical psychology consultant to the Surgeon General of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you also received any medals in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: My most recent decoration was for some contributions that I made in terms of credentials and qualifications for psychologists in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To be kind to the interpreters, Doctor, you can take the earphones off, and if you want to move it to Channel 6 just so that you realise that there is a translation delay between my question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How long have you been licensed to practice psychology?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Since 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In what state are you licensed?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: In the State of California.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you board certified?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. I hold my boards from the American Board of Professional Psychology in clinical psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what board certification means and why it's important?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Board certification is an examination-based process where you submit yourself to peer review, demonstrating a higher level of expertise to your peers that qualifies you for recognition of advanced status, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I currently serve as both a clinical and a forensic psychologist. I specialise in the forensic aspects of psychology, in issues having to do with ethics, standard of care, and trauma and memory work, and in my clinical practice, I have an outpatient clinical practice, where I see individuals in psychotherapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you board certified in any particular area?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I hold my boards in clinical psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is the American Psychological Association?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: The American Psychological Association is an organisation of psychologists in the United States of America, it's a voluntary organisation and it has multiple purposes, but it's designed to integrate the profession of psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you received any honours from the American Psychological Association?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which honours have you received?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Two years ago, I was voted the status of Fellow of the American Psychological Association for my contributions to psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How does one become a Fellow in the American Psychological Association?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Approximately 5 per cent of the membership receives the status of Fellow. It is a peer review process where your credentials and contributions are reviewed at various levels in the organisation and eventually voted on by the Council of Representatives which is the governing body of the American Psychological Association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many members the American Psychological Association has?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Approximately 65.000 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any journal affiliations?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which journal affiliations do you have?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I am a consulting editor for the Journal of Professional Psychology - Research and Practice published by the American Psychological Association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any academic experience?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What academic experience do you have?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I am currently an assistant clinical professor of medical psychology at the University of California, Los Angeles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what is clinical psychology?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Clinical psychology is that aspect of psychology that is applied and is generally designed to assess and/or treat psychological issues and developmental issues or problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So that means -- does that mean that you are treating people?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: You treat people with mental illnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What clinical experience, if any, do you have?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I was trained as a clinical psychologist, did an internship at the VA Palo Alto in clinical psychology, trained also with Stanford University at that time. I left my internship and spent two years as a division psychologist for the 9th Infantry Division of the United States Army, left that capacity, and began employment in an outpatient HMO in Southern California. As I established my private practice in clinical psychology, left the HMO to go into full-time private practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you served on any professional boards or committees?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. I served as a member of the ethics committee of the California Psychological Association for four years, spent the fifth year as the chair of that committee. Following that, I was elected or appointed, if you will, to be a hearing officer for the American Psychological Association, and in that capacity you hear complaints, or cases if you will, and render decisions about ethical conduct. I then was appointed as a fact-finder, now known as an associate, to the ethics committee of the American Psychological Association, spent two years in that capacity and was elected by the Council of Representatives to the committee, served three years on the committee, finishing my last year as chairperson of the ethics committee of the American Psychological Association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What does the ethics committee of the American Psychological Association do?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: It has two functions: one is to enforce the ethical standards of psychologists in a disciplinary fashion on its members, that is, deal with complaints; and then it serves an educative function. It is involved in educating the membership about ethical issues, to include the review and the development of new ethics codes. Although the codes are developed by sub committees, the committee retains authority over the codes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you serve as a consultant for any boards or committees?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which do you serve?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I consult to various licensing boards in the State of California to include the Medical Board, Board of Psychology, Board of Behavioural Sciences, Nursing Board, and other health care boards, and also consult with the Board of Psychology in the State of Nevada on standards of care and ethics issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you published or presented any articles on psychology?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many articles have you published or presented?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I have six peer review publications and a number of other publications in widely disseminated journals, if you will, like the Register Report of the National Register of Psychologists. It's a United States organisation that publishes a journal, if you will, or a newsletter about ethical issues, and I write articles for that and then publications in various division newsletters as well and have made presentations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been qualified as an expert in a Court of law?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In how many cases have you been qualified as an expert?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Approximately 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did your testimony in any of the cases in which you have been qualified as an expert deal with traumatic memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many cases?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: At a minimum three cases: one criminal, one civil, and in another, an administrative law matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your professional practice as a clinical and forensic psychologist, have you worked with cases that involve memory and trauma?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. I have treated trauma victims in my practice and, in my forensic practice, have done extensive assessments of trauma victims, both with established trauma as well as debated trauma, if you will, and so both in the capacity as a forensic psychologist as well as a clinical psychologist I've worked with issues of trauma and memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: During your tenure with the ethics committee of the American Psychological Association, did you deal with cases that involved trauma?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and, in fact, at that time the debate was raging about memory recovery and false memory syndrome, if you will, and that piqued my interest in the area because there were allegations of professional misconduct wrapped around that, and in addition, the American Psychological Association was involved in the preparation of a report about traumatic memory which was published, and so I carried that interest with me after I left the committee and have pursued that interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever treated victims of trauma?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many, approximately, patients of victims of trauma have you treated?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if you start with the beginning of my clinical training and you -- I was at the VA Palo Alto. The majority of the residents there were World War II and Korean War veterans, most of whom were trauma victims. Then I was responsible for dealing with the emotional problems of an infantry division that had just rotated out of Vietnam, full of individuals who were exposed to combat and trauma. I maintained my contact with the military, seeing patients at Letterman Army Medical Centre and Brook Army Medical Centre as well as seeing non-combat trauma victims in my general clinical practice. Although that is not exclusively what I treated, it was a part of my practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you treated any victims of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. I obviously treated victims of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder in the VA in the army. In those days, we didn't have the diagnosis, we just had the problems. Subsequent to that, I have seen individuals who have carried the diagnosis and I've treated them, as well as assessed individuals who have carried that diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever treated rape victims?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. Again, as a part of my clinical practice, I would see rape victims -- to be honest, I think that rape victims generally are better treated by women than men because generally the victims are women, but I would triage with hospitals that I have worked with, and so in that capacity have treated rape victims, and then have seen rape victims in therapy in various capacities over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the field of forensic consulting?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is forensic consulting, and do you have any experience in that area?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, actually, yes, forensic consulting is that aspect of psychology, if you will, forensic psychology, that deals with the application of psychology to the legal process or to an administrative process, testimony, evaluation, disability evaluation, those kinds of things, and I guess in recognition of whether I have expertise in that or not, the American Psychological Association has contracted with me and two other authors to write a book on forensic psychology to be published by the American Psychological Association to help clinicians understand the differences between forensic and clinical psychology and to avoid the pitfalls that exist in crossing those lines, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence offers Dr. Jeffrey Younggren as an expert in the areas of clinical and forensic psychology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, have you reviewed any documents in preparation for this case?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I reviewed the testimony of Witness A, 1993, 1995, 1997, the direct and the cross-examination for this trial; in addition, I reviewed the documents from Medica concerning her treatment; and then I reviewed the documents that the Court has accepted today; and I also reviewed the testimony of Witness D in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with the different methods of treating victims of trauma and rape?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is the primary objective when treating a rape trauma patient?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, the primary objective of treating a rape trauma patient is not a lot different, in a general sense, from treating any kind of patient; that is, you are to try and alleviate the psychological difficulties that they're having. Specifically with trauma, there are certain kinds of techniques that are more effective with that than others and some of which are actually destructive in terms of recovery of patients. But in general, the treatment of trauma victims requires the establishment of a therapeutic relationship and then, in some gradual and supportive way, a working-through or a re-experiencing, if you will, of the traumatic event, to organise it as well as to desensitise to the PTSD symptoms that might be present or to the symptoms of the trauma, that doesn't have to be PTSD, and coupled with that appropriate medication intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the terms "forensic reality" and "emotional reality"?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What do those terms mean?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, it's a term of much discussion in psychology because emotional reality of a patient has to do with their beliefs and what they respond to in their perception of what happened to them and emotional reality is an important part of therapy; that is, a therapist would not necessarily pursue truth, if you will, in a factual sense in order to obtain treatment or to pursue treatment. In fact, if you question a victim too much, it's destructive to the relationship. I would say that short of extreme kinds of allegations, that is, alien abductions and satanic cults, therapists generally accept what a patient brings to them and they work with that and they work with the inconsistencies in it, and that's the emotional reality, vastly different from the forensic reality which has to do with truth, it has to do with the questions that are going on here and in lots of courtrooms about what happened, what didn't happen and so forth. Forensic reality can often be destructive to the emotional reality, and that's why the profession holds the position that treating therapists should not do forensic assessments in the cases that they're treating because they get into mixed roles that can be destructive to the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question before you leave that? That is the American view; those are the guidelines to the American profession?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and truly I think in a general sense they're adopted -- obviously, many countries don't have highly-trained experts and obviously there are constraints as a function of that, but we take very seriously the difference between a forensic role and a clinical role, and mostly for -- you know, frankly for two reasons, one of which is that mixing those roles can be destructive to the patient because if you say what they told you is a lie or you don't believe it, you're not going to be able to be a very good therapist; and the second is that therapists tend to become advocates for patients out of the treatment setting. You're trying to get them better and you bond, we call it transference, that's a generic term, and so a treating therapist is not necessarily objective in a forensic sense so they're not good witnesses in expert testimony. They may be good fact witnesses or treating therapists for fact witnesses but not forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, to follow up on Judge Mumba's question: Do you have any knowledge of whether that standard that you described about the separation between forensic treatment and -- forensic analysis and emotional treatment, whether that is something that is generally accepted outside the borders of the United States? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I don't think that it's a matter of a lot of debate, and I would -- I can't cite you publication citations for it, but the standards I'm sure are accepted in Britain and countries in Europe as well. We just had the International Congress of Psychologists in California and, in fact, I presented to the International Congress on Ethics Issues, so there is an integration of standards going on. I can't say what every country's standard is, but they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, having served on the ethics committee of the American Psychological Association, are you familiar with the minimum standards necessary for someone to begin practice in the area of psychology?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I'm familiar with primarily the standards in the United States of America and a number of countries, not the world standard, but, yes, generally the title "psychologist," if you will, is restricted or at least encouraged to be restricted to people who hold a doctoral degree in psychology. Many states have a master's level psychotherapist licence for independent practice, so it's safe to say that the minimum level of education in the United States for an individual to do psychotherapy independently is a master's degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there a minimum level of experience that a person must have before they attain a licence to practice in the area of psychology?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. In most states, there is both pre-degree and post-degree supervision that's required, anywhere from 1.500 to 3.000 hours. I can't speak for every state, but I've testified in a number of states and discussed their licensing laws, and generally there is a supervision component that is embedded in the licence in addition to the education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, would you recommend that a person with no knowledge about trauma or how to deal with it treat a patient who has Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Individuals who are absent knowledge of trauma may be useful in an emergency sense to give support and help guide or triage someone to a victim, to someone who has experience, but in the hands of an inexperienced therapist, you can do significant emotional damage to someone if you utilise the wrong kinds of therapeutic interventions. You can actually make the symptoms far worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What can happen if a person is not properly treated for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: As I said, you can make the symptoms worse. You can -- the term in the literature is "retraumatise" them and it's really regressive. It just creates a whole another set of problems or makes the problems more severe, so the therapy is not helpful. I mean, this is an area of substantial reading, and individuals who work in it and treat victims need to have some knowledge of both the psychological and psychiatric and even some of the new medical literature coming out about neurology of PTSD victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What effects, if any, could trauma have on memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I am willing to acknowledge that this is a matter of debate in the profession and I'm sure that you will hear individuals take a different position on this, but my reading of the literature indicates that trauma can have effect on memory. Generally memory is good, but that there are studies, Southwicke's research, Koss's research, that indicate that trauma has effects on memory in various ways different from experiencing of unpleasant events by individuals who have not been traumatised, so I'm one of those individuals that believes that the debate goes on but that there is some very good research that shows that the more trauma you have, the worse your memory is, and specifically can cite the research for that. So it's a matter of debate, but there is evidence that trauma affects memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you say that there is a debate. Is there a debate among the various psychological associations on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I really believe that, for example, in the area of repressed memories, which is not a matter in this case, the American Psychological Association, the American Psychiatric Association, and the British Society have all taken very conservative positions about the validity of those memories and caution clinicians who work with them to be most careful about assuming those memories to be true and assuming positions of advocacy because of those memories. So the associations have taken conservative views. There are divisions among various groups in psychology about the accuracy of memory and the debate goes on, but as I said, my reading of the literature, my belief is that there is data to show that trauma affects memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to quote you a few lines out of Defence 22 which is the document titled "Medica Psycho Team." It's page 2, under the heading of "Retrospect." "At the beginning of our work over two years ago, we often felt helpless. We had no knowledge about trauma and how to deal with it. We ourselves didn't know how we should cope with our own traumatic experiences or how we could protect ourselves internally against the terrible stories we heard each day." And then that very next paragraph: "At first, we lacked experience and theoretical knowledge, but our daily work and the discussions with women taught us quickly and we became increasingly confident." Doctor, in this particular case, given what you've just testified to, could Medica's lack -- or lack of knowledge about trauma and how to deal with it, its lack of experience or theoretical knowledge have had an effect on Witness A's memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Absolutely. It could have had an effect and it could have led to contamination of memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is contamination of memory and how does that apply in this case?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, contamination of memory is where individuals functionally begin to believe things that are not true, can be the result of them filling in blanks from information given to them by other people or piecing memory fragments together in ways that are not necessarily truthful. Again, they may be emotionally meaningful but you may create a belief system that can be dangerous. In addition, if these individuals engage in techniques that retraumatise or encourage things like confrontation, it can be destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, if a therapist starts acts as an advocate with a patient and lacks knowledge about trauma and how to deal with it, or experience, what type of consequences could result?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I think if you limit your advocacy to the treatment setting, and I've said that's important, that's helpful. If you advocate beliefs in things that are wrong, that can be very destructive. I'll give a case in point that I've been involved in, a lady who was -- had a very disturbed psychological history. We would say she had a personality disorder -- went into therapy with an individual who was a believer in cults and satanic cults, if you will. The analysis of the transcriptions of the therapy, as well as the therapist's consultation with other people indicate that belief was reinforced. The patient developed a belief that she was a birthing mother for a satanic cult, if you will, and deteriorated emotionally, was hospitalised and actually involved in some very serious criminal allegations. But the point is that when they did a gynaecological examination on her, her hymen was still intact. Now, somehow what she believed, and I believe came from the process of her therapy with someone who was inexperienced, didn't help her at all, and substantially complicated her life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what the method of group therapy is?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Group therapy is the treatment modality where you put together individuals, usually who suffer some kind of homogenous problem, in a setting with a therapist to work on those problems in various ways. Usually one or two therapists and a number of group members, and it's a verbal exchange therapy usually. I mean, there are group therapies for relaxation and so forth, but group therapy is group therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What effect or effects, if any, might group therapy have on memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Again, as I said earlier, I have concerns that that kind of a therapy fills in the blanks, if you will, and can create false beliefs. It might be useful for those false beliefs or peripheral false beliefs, less so than with the gist memories, but some of the detail memories could be altered. And that, frankly, could be helpful from a treatment perspective but might not be helpful in another setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by that last comment?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: As I said earlier, it may help a patient to put that together and then talk about their problems in an environment where they can relax, and accept them and make therapeutic progress, but then to take those beliefs out and bring them out as fact in terms of confronting people, which is an issue for -- in the profession, and/or coming to a forum like a courtroom and saying they're factual, it's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you know what guided imagery therapy is?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is guided imagery therapy?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, first let me say, people do guided imagery therapy differently, but it has to do with a model of therapy where an individual is generally relaxed and then encouraged to fantasise either in a passive way with the therapist, or some therapists actively participate in helping the patient imagine things, usually to piece together improved memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in this case, again I'm using D22, page 3, it describes some of the techniques that were used at Medica to treat patients. Just above the title "Safety in a War," it says: "At the same time we found suitable therapeutic techniques with which we could back up our ideas. These included relaxation methods, dreamed and imagined journeys, breathing techniques and work with the body. Our self-confidence also grew at the same rate as our knowledge and our assessment of our experiences as the results of our work improved." My question to you, Doctor, is if Medica were engaging in the methods of treatment that are described in that citation, and they lacked the experience or knowledge in the treatment of trauma patients, how could this have affected Witness A's memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, assuming that Witness A participated in this, this could have contributed to false beliefs in terms of what happened. I think that relaxation therapy is not -- I wouldn't criticise that, that's a helpful therapy. I would worry about what "dreamed and imagined journeys" mean. Dreams are not necessarily truthful mind adventures, journeys, and imagined journeys concerns me. It's awfully close to what I was talking about, although I'm not sure. Breathing techniques may be relaxation, which is fine, and I don't know what work with the body is, but it does worry me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is -- just so we're clear on this, what is the dream journey technique, or what is dream therapy?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly they do, but dream journeys and dream interpretation is, frankly, an analysis of people's dreams to determine what they mean. Frequently individuals will encourage that those dreams are representations of what occurred coming from the unconscious mind. I don't think that's supported by the empirical literature at all, but that is a kind of a common lay belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You talked earlier about the objective of therapy being the recovery of the patient. How does this objective affect reported memory, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, depends upon how it's used. The -- I mean, if you're talking about someone developing memories that are generally accurate, somewhat inaccurate, and the end result of that would help them recover, to put meaning to what occurred to them and to learn to cope with those experiences and thoughts of what occurred in more adaptive ways, to accept the reality, it can be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you seen any evidence of this in this particular case, in terms of the primary objective possibly affecting reported memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I have some concerns about it. One of the concerns I have is the mixed mission of Medica. In their position statement they say that their goal is to deal with war criminals, and I believe that's in one of the documents, and that may be incompatible with the recovery of patients. So if that is a goal that's carried into the treatment setting, and again, I don't know if it was or wasn't, but assuming that's the mission, then it may encourage patients to do things that are not necessarily treatment oriented, if you will, or recovery oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, so we're clear on that cite, that reference that you just made, I'm going to give you the following passage and ask you if that was the cite you were referring to. I believe it's D25. It is the document entitled, "BosNews Report - Medica Zenica Women Therapy Centre," and it is page 5 under the subtitle "Research." It states: "While our mobile teams visit..." that's in the original, "...the refugee camps, they also collect data on refugees in order to understand and analyse the full dimension of war violence against women in ex-Yugoslavia, summon international law courts against war criminals and contribute to the world-wide feminist analysis of patriarchal violence in war." Is that the passage that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes, it concerns me as a clinician. The goal of arriving at a legal conclusion may not be compatible with the recovery of some trauma patients. It might be for some trauma patients too, but that kind of a patient-by-patient -- that would require a patient-by-patient analysis, so I can see where there might be a conflict of interest in Medica's goal here with what their treatment goals are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is there any specific research that has been conducted on the memories of rape victims?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. There's a substantial amount of research on the memory of rape victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what do those studies reveal?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Again, many of those studies get into the remember-don't remember war, but there is one impressive study by Koss in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology that says rape victims suffer memory detriment in terms of clarity and affect effects, as opposed to other individuals who have negative experiences, or to individuals who don't necessarily have negative experiences. It is a very good study to show, I believe, that rape, as an individual type of trauma, has effects on memory. It's from the University of Arizona.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does this research indicate -- or what, if anything, does this research indicate about accuracy for visual details, like appearance of others?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, there's an implication in it that individuals who have been victims of rape may, in fact, have less accurate memories and clarity of what occurred, and so I don't think it's a big leap to conclude that that would apply to visual details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could that inaccuracy in visual details, having read the witness statements in this case, do you see -- what, if any, application do you see for that in this case?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's striking that Witness A initially had a recollection of the defendant as blonde and short, when, in fact, he clearly isn't blonde and short, and that that shift is, at least in my reading, very evident in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you able to make an opinion as to the psychological makeup of Witness A?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No. I couldn't do that without conducting a psychological evaluation of her, and I wouldn't be qualified because I don't speak Croatian. For a variety of reasons, but most importantly is I haven't evaluated her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is the confidence a patient displays about memories an indicator of reliability?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No. It's a measure of confidence. People can be very confident about things that occurred that simply hadn't occurred. Again, not necessarily the gist of what occurred, but confident about some details and be very wrong. I think all of us have experienced that at least some way or another in our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what indication, if any, of that have you seen in this case?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I've read the testimony of Witness A, I have -- I've observed her testimony. There's no question she went through a horrific trauma, and she is impressively confident in her beliefs and purpose, and I hope this process is helpful to her to recover from what occurred, but a confidence doesn't mean that she's right. It doesn't mean she's wrong either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You believe the memories of your own patients?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Generally, yes, because of what I spoke about earlier. It is an important part of treatment. Unless you get into those extreme areas where I think that it's not helpful for people to carry around bizarre beliefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to your own patients, do you believe that the memories of trauma reported to you from your trauma patients are forensically accurate, that is factually accurate?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I believe their memories are emotionally accurate. I don't even deal with the forensic end of it. I'm working with the patient to help that individual recover from emotional distress. That's my goal, and if I didn't believe it, it would affect my therapeutic alliance in relationships that is so very important to therapy. It would have lots of negative effects. So from the emotional perspective, we're in the belief together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if you were asked to -- or if you wanted to make a forensic conclusion about one of your patients, that is a factual conclusion, how could you determine the factual accuracy?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I wouldn't go there. I mean, I really -- that's, as far as I'm concerned, a ethics violation, because I've lost my objectivity. I'm an advocate for the patient and I have beliefs consistent with the patient's beliefs, and that is simply not necessarily a forensic reality. I would be willing to share that information with the forensic evaluator who is working for the Court, or for lawyers, to make that determination, but because I'm a treating therapist, it precludes me from testifying as a forensic expert about truth, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Younggren. I have nothing further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. We have a few minutes. Perhaps the Prosecution could start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you just give me one minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just do one or two matters this afternoon. I understand our time period is down. The Prosecution would like to offer into evidence the document entitled, "Reply, The Medica Centre for Treatment of Women." The Defence, I believe, has indicated earlier that they would agree to its authentication. We'd like to ask our learned colleagues to allow us to submit this into evidence as we have priorly submitted their other documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was that document submitted? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit 5, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we have copies for the Court also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Am I to understand now that the document will be admitted into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's admitted as P5. We're being told that it's the same document as D24.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm talking about the reply from the Medica centre. I believe that the Defence entered into evidence the report of the Medica centre. Your Honour, am I to believe that the reply is part of the document that's been submitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If it's part of our document, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The whole document was submitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We need to need to raise one procedural matter, and I apologise. With respect to the order of sequestration of witnesses, et cetera, I'm not clear as to whether that would apply in the expert context. We have no objection if during the breaks they wish to consult with their experts, and the reason we say that is otherwise, we're have to ostracise Dr. Younggren tonight and leave him alone someplace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. With experts it doesn't matter really. If counsel wishes to consult, they can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we're dealing with this document. You say the whole document, including the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So just withdraw P5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's part of D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Leave it as D24.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Younggren.

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: End of the afternoon, I imagine. Dr. Younggren, you've testified about your relationships to standard of care and standard of practice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you have been involved for over 20 years with questions of ethics and the standard of care in California; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as an expert, you're involved in handling compliance that could lead to either someone's licence being revoked or turned over to the State Attorney General in California; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I imagine that whenever you evaluate a complaint, there are certain steps that you take before reaching the decision that you'll transmit to the licensing board; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For example, before you would reach a conclusion, you would probably study the psychologist's file; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: If that's in the evidence. Basically if you need information, you can request it, or you need to limit or qualify your statement to the documents that you've reviewed, but you either get more information or you have the information with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Because the information would be important in terms of trying to reach that decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And at times would you request to speak to that psychologist if you needed information?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Actually, no. The boards generally don't want you to do that. I don't establish the procedures, but if you want information, an investigator will go out and do that. On occasion you will speak to the psychologist, but generally not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So generally you have information from the psychologist through the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would there be certain questions that you would ask that investigator to inquire of that psychologist?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you ask them what type of therapy was given?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Depending upon the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you ask them what types of techniques were used in that particular therapy?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Once again, depending upon the case, yes. And the reason I qualify is, there are some violations that it doesn't make any difference what kind of therapy you did, but generally when one talks about certain kinds of interventions, what they do is very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Particularly when we're talking about the standard of care; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I would imagine that you would then evaluate whatever information the investigator brought back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, what types of techniques would you inquire about before you'd reach a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: An evaluation consists of a review of the information, and then a citation of relevant literature having to do with the standard of care, codes, laws, local standards of practice, and an integration of those into a decision. And again, if the decision is qualified, and by that I mean frequently the cases do not include a defence because an attorney has advised the individual not to provide that to the medical board or psychology board, and so you basically say, assuming these materials are true, then this is my conclusion. Obviously, if there is other information, you reserve the right to qualify the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Am I correct in assuming that in the case we have before us today, that you did not talk to the psychologist?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Actually, I don't know who the psychologist is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you didn't talk to the psychologist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I also assume that you did not send an investigator to ask about the techniques or the therapy that was used?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I actually asked if there was more information and was informed that that was not available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Whom did you ask?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand. Then I imagine you at least got a copy of the local standards of care practised within the former Yugoslavia, the Zenica region?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you able to inquire whether one was available, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you've given forensic testimony concerning a criminal case before, in terms of memory?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: An administrative case?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And a civil case?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How many other criminal cases, sir, have you given forensic evidence in?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I believe three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let's say a total of four criminal cases, and one of those criminal cases, sir, dealt with the question of memory and trauma; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, memory and trauma -- one, two -- three of them are trauma cases. So three out of five are trauma cases, one memory-trauma case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you've actually testified in one case concerning memory and trauma to date?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: One criminal case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Prior to today, of course?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Younggren, I understand that your focus, from your CV, is on ethics, isn't that correct, not memory and trauma?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Actually, I spend a great amount of time working with memory and trauma, and I would say the majority of my forensic assessments have been simply on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Not the ones you've testified in court about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Most of them are civil cases and they've settled.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I've enjoyed looking at your CV. You have a long list of publications and most of those are concerning ethics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You've mentioned that you will have a book that's coming out, but to date I do not see any publications concerning memory or trauma, or memory or rape; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Actually, that is correct. It's not an area that I publish in, except in terms of comments about the risk to professionals who work in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, also I noticed on your CV that you have not listed any of the rape crisis centres in which you have worked at. Have you worked at a rape crisis centre?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you consulted directly with a rape crisis centre, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Well, I worked with the Los Angeles Free Clinic that saw rape cases, it was a generic clinic. Then I had rape cases at the HMO that I worked at as well, but I didn't work at a rape crisis centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you supervised therapists who have worked at rape crisis centres?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I see that you reviewed many of the materials, I imagine, that are relevant to this case. I would like to know, in that review of materials, because you furnished that to the Prosecution, isn't it correct that most of the materials that you informed us that you reviewed dealt with questions of childhood sexual abuse?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would object. Give the witness a copy of the document. I believe he said there is nothing particular that he reviewed for this case, however, there are books about the area that may be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm referring to a document supplied to us by the Defence concerning the materials that Dr. Younggren was going to rely upon, attached to the different studies. Then I assume Dr. Younggren knew of the list of materials that you had forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, I would prefer that we have the document we're talking about, because that was my comment before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Which document in particular?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, maybe I can refresh your memory. You cited the book of Dr. Elizabeth Loftus?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Younggren, the book of Dr. Elizabeth Loftus, that book basically deals with recovered memories during childhood abuse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: It's the major theme, but it is a publication about memory trauma and recovery from trauma. I mean, it's a memory book, but the primary topic is child sexual abuse and repressed memories.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And Dr. Younggren, you also refer to another work entitled, "Validation of Sexual Abuse in Day Care Settings."

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: Right. That's Dr. Fisher's publication, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, is that work also about sexual abuse of children?

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: It actually has to do with applying the ethics codes to arriving at conclusions about sexual abuse in areas where there's not existing literature, so it's -- but the topic is children, obviously, by the title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, I think we've reached our break-off point, 17.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll be able to continue this discussion tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JEFFREY NELS YOUNGGREN
utterances.text: I will be here, counsellor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 5.35 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of November, 1998 at 9:30 a.m.
